props.title: The Kid Stays in the Picture

sections.content: The Kid Stays in the Picture (2002) revolutionized documentary filmmaking with its innovative visual approach to telling Hollywood producer Robert Evans' larger-than-life story. Directors Nanette Burstein and Brett Morgen transformed Evans' audiobook into a kaleidoscopic journey through New Hollywood, using 2.5D photo animation that influenced countless documentaries after it. The film charts Evans' meteoric rise from failed actor to Paramount's head of production, where he shepherded classics like Rosemary's Baby (1968), The Godfather (1972), and Chinatown (1974).

sections.content: The documentary's style perfectly mirrors Evans' flashy persona and Hollywood's seductive power. The filmmakers layer archival photos, creating a pseudo-3D effect that makes still images feel alive and dynamic. This technique, combined with Evans' own gravelly narration, creates an intoxicating portrait of 1970s Hollywood excess. His brutal honesty about both triumphs (Love Story (1970)) and disasters (The Cotton Club (1984)) set a new standard for entertainment industry documentaries.

Evans' story intersects with every major figure of New Hollywood - from his friendship with Jack Nicholson to his battles with Francis Ford Coppola. The film shows how one charismatic producer helped transform American cinema in the 1970s, backing artistically ambitious films that were also commercial hits. His cocaine-fueled fall from grace parallels the end of that golden era, making this both a personal story and a crucial document of Hollywood history. movies.slug: Documentary chronicling the chaotic making of Apocalypse Now, showing the dark side of New Hollywood ambition

sections.content: The film's innovative visual techniques influenced a wave of documentaries that followed, including Searching for Sugar Man (2012) and Man on Wire (2008). The way it brings photos to life through motion and depth created a new visual language for biographical documentaries. Evans' unvarnished narration of his own story - including his failures and regrets - established a template for celebrity self-examination that documentaries still follow today.
